blocks.x: This fall, there’s no shortage of exciting new cookbooks. Ina Garten is back with her 14th title, which is all about smart streamlining because store-bought is fine. Yotam Ottolenghi is dipping back into simple cooking with a sequel to his popular 2018 title, Ottolenghi Simple. And Lucas Sin is transporting us to Hong Kong’s iconic diners. The heavy hitters came to play! Read on for more standout titles of the season (organized by release date), handpicked and cooked from by our staff.
No. 1 Best Indian Cookbook in the World by Meherwan Irani

After a spellbinding meal at chef Meherwan Irani’s Chai Pani in Washington, DC, and many years spent electrifying my taste buds with his Spicewalla blends, I leapt at the chance to crack open Irani’s debut cookbook. His recipes and stories in it showcase a broad perspective on Indian cuisine and a career spent championing it for American audiences. The book is a riot, saturated with rich color and food, and sprinkled with hilarious commentary like “naan pisses me off.” Recipe titles like The Obligatory Saag Paneer hint at myopic expectations for Indian menus, yet Irani still offers a compelling (unblended!) version. I made the Tandoori Chicken, which is adapted for home cooks lacking a tandoor, the hot clay oven. Irani has you roast the meat at a high temperature, then give it a stint under the broiler for wonderful char. Masala Omelet Sandos are packed with layers of aromatics like onion, green chiles, and turmeric, and topped with a gooey mesmerizing layer of American cheese. —Chris Morocco, food director

Bake Anything by Erin Jeanne McDowell

As the saying goes, “A good teacher explains, a superior teacher demonstrates, and a great teacher inspires.” But what happens when you do all three? Erin Jeanne McDowell, the author of the seminal The Book on Pie, is no stranger to walking readers through complex baked goods and making the recipes feel achievable. Her fourth and latest book, Bake Anything, is designed to be the “building blocks of baking.” With foundational techniques, recipes are padded out with flavor variations (she offers nine different pudding ideas), storage tips (you can freeze frosting!), and even customized yields, showcasing the wide and wondrous world of sweets and treats. The Victoria Sponge Sheet Cake I made was buxom, with an otherworldly airy crumb. —Shilpa Uskokovic, senior Test Kitchen editor

Gather Around My Table by Kay Chun

Known for her former NYC restaurant, Share, and stellar recipe development chops, I couldn’t wait to cook through Kay Chun’s debut book, Gather Around My Table. True to its title, Chun’s ethos is simple: The best cooking is all about connection. That spirit pulses through her stories: Chun shares fond childhood memories of wrapping dumplings with her mother and grandmother and regularly eating global plates of food; she was just as likely to devour Kalbi jjim (Korean braised short ribs) as she was meatloaf. “Eating this way taught me that exciting flavor comes in many forms and often from their combination,” she writes. That sensibility shines in her recipes. Kimchi brine gives her micheladas a spicy, electric lift, and earthy kale and savory seaweed lend her risotto depth. Also: doenjang carnitas. How fun is that? —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

Ottolenghi Simple Too by Yotam Ottolenghi

I’ve long been a fan of chef Yotam Ottoglenghi’s flavorful recipes; but on busy weeknights I simply don’t have the energy to cook dishes with lengthy ingredient lists. This is exactly why I loved his 2018 book, Ottolenghi Simple, and I was delighted to see this year’s follow-up, Ottolenghi Simple Too. Cowritten with Verena Lochmuller, with additional contributions by Milli Taylor and Tara Wigley, the book picks up where the original left off. “‘Simple’ means something different to everyone,” Ottolenghi writes in the introduction. “For some, that’s cooking dinner in half an hour. For others, it’s about a slow-cooking dish that bubbles away while they’re in the garden.” The book keeps ingredient lists low (at about 10), the techniques straightforward, and the active time minimal. In the Test Kitchen, our team couldn’t get enough of the Salmon With Apricot and Cilantro Pesto (the sauce would be just as good over chicken or steak). And the Braised Halloumi With Tomatoes and Beans has become a new weeknight go-to go for me. —Rebecca Firkser, Test Kitchen editor

blocks.x: Daily Dessert by Caroline Schiff

Those lucky enough to have tasted Caroline Schiff’s creations at Gage & Tollner, where she led the pastry team, have been eagerly anticipating her second cookbook. Daily Dessert shows off what Schiff does best: injecting savory ingredients into sweets and creating desserts that are both nostalgic and unlike anything you’ve ever tasted. When I made her Sage Brown Butter Loaf in the Test Kitchen, team members marveled at the quick bread’s tender texture and herbal quintessence. Equally compelling is the way Schiff has laid out this book: There is a chapter on desserts for two (or one!), including a mini tiramisu and a single pecan blondie (served warm with butterscotch sauce). The next chapter is for desserts you “Bake Once, Snack All Week.” The flavors—and imagination—are every bit as big as her iconic hair. —Joe Sevier, senior SEO editor, cooking

East to East by Rachel Gurjar

East to East transports you from former BA staffer Rachel Gurjar’s hometown in Mumbai all the way to New York, where she now lives and works as a chef and tastemaker. Gurjar writes from a reflective, earnest place about navigating the two cities—the significance of cultural preservation, and how cooking brought her closer to herself. This intimate storytelling sits alongside a range of recipes: traditional family ones and thoughtful riffs on American classics. I made the Indian Fried Chicken and Coconut Key Lime Pie, two dishes that encapsulate one of the things Gurjar does well: make things her own. Every culture has its own fried chicken, but this one is special; it has a garlicky spice mix, a yogurt marinade that powerfully tenderizes the meat, and a topping of fried curry leaves for a fragrant boost. The pie had an extra-tangy custard and finely grated coconut in the crust—an addition that will make you wonder why you’ve never thought to do it sooner. —Inés Anguiano, associate Test Kitchen manager
